lessons.title: Planning input requirements
lessons.html:
Knowing what you need before you buy

Agricultural inputs are everything the farm uses to produce: seed, fertiliser, lime, agricultural remedies, animal feed, vaccines and medicines, fuel, packaging, spares and small tools. Inputs are often the largest part of variable costs, so careful procurement has a direct effect on profit.

Working out quantities

Start from the production plan. For each enterprise, list the area or animal numbers and the recommended rate. For example, 80 ha of maize at the fertiliser rate recommended from soil analysis, or 20 000 broilers using the feed amounts in the breeder's guide per bird. Add a small allowance for losses but avoid large overstocks. Check what is already in the store before ordering.

Timing

Draw up an input calendar showing when each input is needed in the field. Plan orders so stock arrives in time, taking account of supplier lead times. Fertiliser and seed for summer crops are often in short supply close to planting, and prices may rise. Ordering early can secure stock and better prices, but money tied up in stock costs interest, so balance timing with the cash flow budget.

Specification

Write clear specifications: product name and grade, pack size, quantity, delivery date and place. For seed, specify cultivar or hybrid and seed treatment. For agricultural remedies, use only products registered under Act 36 of 1947 for that crop and pest, as recommended by a registered adviser. For vet medicines, follow your vet's programme.

Example

A farm plans 80 ha of maize and finds 4 tons of fertiliser left over in the store from last season. The order is reduced by that amount, and the planner checks the bags are still dry and usable before counting them.

lessons.title: Buying inputs
lessons.html:
Getting value from suppliers

Choosing suppliers

Get quotes from at least two or three suppliers for major items: co-operatives, agri-dealers and direct from manufacturers. Compare more than price:

  • Product quality and whether it meets the specification
  • Delivery time and reliability
  • Payment terms, such as 30 days or harvest credit through a co-op
  • Technical support from the supplier's agronomist or animal health adviser
  • Discounts for volume, early orders or group buying with neighbours

Purchase controls

  1. Use a written order or purchase order with an order number for every purchase.
  2. Get approval from the person authorised to sign for that amount.
  3. Keep copies of quotes so the choice can be explained.
  4. Check the invoice against the order and the delivery note before payment.

These controls prevent fraud, duplicate payments and buying things nobody approved.

Receiving deliveries

When inputs arrive, count and check them against the delivery note. Check expiry dates on remedies, vaccines and medicines. Check seed bags for the correct cultivar and treatment, and fertiliser for torn or wet bags. Record any shortages or damage on the delivery note before signing and tell the supplier the same day. Vaccines must go straight into the fridge at the right temperature.

Example

Two co-ops quote for 30 tons of fertiliser. Co-op A is R150 per ton cheaper but can only deliver after planting has started. Co-op B delivers in time and offers harvest credit. Co-op B is the better choice, because late fertiliser costs far more in lost yield than the price difference. Record the reason for the decision with the quotes.

lessons.title: Storing and controlling inputs
lessons.html:
Protecting the farm's money in the store

Storage rules

  • Agricultural remedies: a locked, ventilated store with a bunded floor, away from food, feed and water sources, with warning signs, spill kit and fire extinguisher. Only trained people have the key.
  • Fertiliser: dry, on pallets, away from fuel and heat. Some fertilisers are fire or explosion risks; follow the safety data sheet.
  • Seed and feed: dry, cool, on pallets, protected from rodents and birds.
  • Vaccines and medicines: in a fridge with a thermometer, recorded daily if required.
  • Fuel: in approved tanks in a bunded area, no smoking, with fire extinguishers nearby.

Stock control

Keep a stock register or use the farm system. Record every item received and every item issued, with date, quantity, who took it and for which block, enterprise or vehicle. Use the first in, first out rule so older stock is used before it expires. Do a physical stock count every month and compare it with the register. Investigate differences straight away.

Managing use

Compare input use with the plan. If a block used much more fertiliser than planned, find out why: a calibration error, a wrong rate or theft. Report usage per enterprise to management because it feeds directly into gross margins and the next year's budget.

Key points

  • Base input quantities on the production plan and check stock before ordering.
  • Compare suppliers on quality, delivery, terms and support, not only price.
  • Use purchase orders and check invoices against orders and delivery notes.
  • Store remedies locked and away from food, feed and water; keep vaccines cold.
  • Record all receipts and issues, use first in first out, and count stock monthly.

quiz.question: Where should you start when working out input quantities?

options.text: The production plan with areas, animal numbers and rates

quiz.question: What should be checked before paying a supplier's invoice?

options.text: That it matches the order and the delivery note
That it is printed in colour

quiz.question: What does 'first in, first out' mean in a store?

options.text: Stock is issued only on Mondays
Older stock is used before newer stock
The first worker to arrive gets stock

quiz.question: Where must vaccines be placed when they are delivered?

options.text: On a pallet in the shed
Straight into a fridge at the correct temperature

quiz.question: What should you do if a delivery is short?

options.text: Sign and sort it out next month
Record the shortage on the delivery note and tell the supplier the same day
